etymology: Hebrew Heman, “faithful” or “trusty,” the chief singer of David, a Kohathite and grandson of Samuel.
biblical_def: Heman was one of the three chief musicians whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, with Asaph and Jeduthun. He was a Kohathite, the son of Joel and grandson of Samuel the prophet (1Ch 6:33), and he is called “the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn” (1Ch 25:5). To him God gave fourteen sons and three daughters, all of them set under their father’s hand for song in the house of God, sounding the cymbals, psalteries, and harps (1Ch 25:5–6). Heman and his company were appointed to prophesy with their instruments and to give thanks to the LORD, “because his mercy endureth for ever” (1Ch 16:41). His ministry was no mere music but a prophetic praise, the lifting up of the horn of God’s people in worship. He is often identified with Heman the Ezrahite, to whom the dark and pleading eighty-eighth Psalm is ascribed. Heman stands at the head of the great tradition of sacred song in Israel, a man whose name means “faithful,” and whose house was given to the LORD that the praise of God might never cease in His courts.
webster_summary: A chief singer of David, a Kohathite and grandson of Samuel, called the king’s seer; father of fourteen sons set to song.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the song of God’s house is a prophetic and holy ministry, not mere ornament. Heman was the king’s seer, set to prophesy with harps and to lift up the horn in praise; his music was the proclaiming of the words of God. The worship of song is a serious and appointed service, by which the truth of God is sung into the hearts of His people.

Heman’s house, given wholly to the song of the LORD, also commends the devoting of a family to the service of God. His fourteen sons stood under his hand in the courts of God’s house, that the praise of God might never cease. It is a great blessing when a household is consecrated to the worship of the LORD, and the gifts of one generation are handed to the next for His glory.

etymology: Hebrew Yeduthun, perhaps “praising” or “giving thanks,” one of the three chief musicians of David.
biblical_def: Jeduthun was one of the three chief musicians whom David appointed over the song of the house of the LORD, with Asaph and Heman. He and his sons were set apart to prophesy with harps, psalteries, and cymbals, and to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1Ch 25:1, 3). The sons of Jeduthun — Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah — ministered under the hand of their father, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD (1Ch 25:3). Jeduthun and Heman were chosen with the rest to give thanks “because his mercy endureth for ever” (1Ch 16:41). His name appears also in the titles of certain Psalms, which are committed “to Jeduthun” for their singing (the thirty-ninth, sixty-second, and seventy-seventh). He is thought by some to be the same as Ethan the Merarite named among the first appointed singers. Jeduthun stands, with Asaph and Heman, at the fountainhead of the sacred music of Israel, a man whose house was devoted to the praise of God, and whose very name, linked to thanksgiving, was fulfilled in the ministry he and his sons rendered before the LORD in His house.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the appointed and prophetic character of thanksgiving in the worship of God. Jeduthun and his sons were separated to prophesy with their instruments and to give thanks to the LORD because His mercy endures for ever. Praise is not a casual addition to worship but a holy and ordered service; the giving of thanks is itself a proclaiming of God’s steadfast mercy.

Jeduthun’s name, linked to thanksgiving, was fulfilled in his life’s work, and his house was devoted to the praise of God across generations. The dictionary marks how the LORD honours the families that consecrate their gifts to His worship; the song begun by Jeduthun was carried on by his sons under his hand, that the thanks of God’s people might rise continually in His courts.

etymology: Hebrew Ethan, “enduring” or “perpetual,” a wise man and singer to whom the eighty-ninth Psalm is ascribed.
biblical_def: Ethan the Ezrahite was a man renowned for wisdom in ancient Israel, named in the Scripture as one whom Solomon’s wisdom exceeded: “he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda” (1Ki 4:31). To Ethan is ascribed the eighty-ninth Psalm, a great meditation on the covenant the LORD made with David, mingling high praise of God’s faithfulness with a bewildered lament that the throne seemed cast down (Ps 89). He is also reckoned among the first singers appointed by David, Ethan the son of Kushaiah of the Merarites, who with Heman and Asaph sounded the cymbals (1Ch 15:17, 19); some take this Ethan to be the same as Jeduthun. His name, “enduring” or “perpetual,” fits the great theme of his Psalm, which clings to the perpetual covenant of God even when His promises seem to fail. Ethan the Ezrahite stands as a witness that true wisdom is found not in the proud knowledge of the world but in the fear of the LORD and the meditation on His covenant; and that faith may wrestle honestly with God’s dark providences while still holding fast to His sure and everlasting word.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faith of the eighty-ninth Psalm, which praises the everlasting faithfulness of God and yet pours out a perplexed lament that the throne of David seemed cast to the ground. Ethan does not resolve the tension by doubting God’s word; he holds the promise fast even in the dark. True faith may wrestle honestly with God’s hard providences and still cling to His sure and perpetual covenant.

Ethan’s renown for wisdom, exceeded only by Solomon, also teaches that the highest wisdom is bound up with the fear of the LORD and the meditation on His covenant, not with the proud knowledge of the world. The wise men of old whom Solomon surpassed were known for a wisdom that fed on the works and ways of God; and even their greatness was a shadow of the wisdom that is in Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

etymology: Hebrew Qehath, perhaps “assembly” or “congregation,” the second son of Levi and father of the most honoured Levitical house.
biblical_def: Kohath was the second son of Levi (Gen 46:11), and the head of the Kohathites, the most honoured of the three great Levitical families. From Kohath came Amram, and from Amram came Aaron, Moses, and Miriam; so the priesthood itself and the leadership of the exodus sprang from his line. To the Kohathites was given the charge of the most holy things of the tabernacle: the ark, the table, the candlestick, the altars, and the vessels of the sanctuary, which they were to bear upon their shoulders after Aaron and his sons had covered them. Yet they were warned that they should not touch any holy thing, lest they die (Num 4:15), so that even the highest Levitical honour was hedged about with holy fear. Kohath lived an hundred thirty and three years (Ex 6:18). His house held both the glory and the danger of nearness to holy things, for from it came the high priests, but also Korah, who rebelled against Moses and Aaron and perished. Kohath stands at the head of the family closest to the worship of God, a witness that the nearest place to the sanctuary is the place of the greatest honour and the greatest accountability before the LORD.
webster_summary: The second son of Levi, head of the Kohathites who bore the most holy things; ancestor of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the nearest place to the sanctuary is the place of greatest honour and greatest accountability. The Kohathites bore the most holy things, yet were warned not to touch them lest they die. High privilege in the service of God is hedged about with holy fear; those who come nearest to sacred things must handle them with the deepest reverence, for honour and danger are joined at the altar.

Kohath’s house held both the high priests and Korah the rebel, the glory and the warning of nearness to holy things. From his line came the priesthood and the leaders of the exodus; from it also came Korah, who despised his Levitical honour and grasped at the priesthood, and perished. The lesson is solemn: to be near the holy is no safety in itself, for the same nearness that exalts the faithful destroys the presumptuous.

etymology: Hebrew Gershon, “a stranger” or “exile there,” the eldest son of Levi.
biblical_def: Gershon, also called Gershom, was the eldest son of Levi (Gen 46:11), and the head of the Gershonites, one of the three great Levitical families. To the Gershonites was given the charge of the coverings and curtains of the tabernacle: the hangings, the curtains of the court, the coverings of the tent, and the cords thereof, which they carried in the wilderness journeys upon two wagons drawn by oxen, under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron (Num 4:24–28; 7:7). Theirs was the service of the fabric of the sanctuary, the soft and outer things that clothed and enclosed the holy place, while the Kohathites bore the inner vessels and the Merarites the framework. When the Levites received cities among the tribes, the Gershonites were given thirteen cities in the north (Josh 21:6). Gershon’s name, “a stranger there,” recalls the pilgrim character of all the tribe of Levi, who had no inheritance among their brethren but the LORD Himself for their portion. Gershon stands at the head of the family charged with the curtains of God’s house, a witness that no part of the service of the sanctuary is too lowly to be a holy charge, and that the LORD assigns to each of His servants his appointed burden.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his house witnesses that no part of the service of God is too lowly to be a holy charge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of every appointed service in the house of God. The Gershonites bore the curtains and coverings, the soft outer things of the tabernacle, while others bore the ark and the framework; yet their charge was holy, and the LORD assigned it to them by name. No part of the service of God is too lowly to be a sacred trust; the humblest task in His house is honourable when done unto Him.

Gershon’s name, “a stranger there,” recalls the pilgrim character of the whole tribe of Levi, who had no inheritance among their brethren but the LORD Himself for their portion. So the servants of God are strangers and pilgrims in the earth, whose true inheritance is the LORD. The Gershonite who carried the curtains through the wilderness is a figure of every saint who journeys as a stranger toward the rest of God.

etymology: Hebrew Merari, “bitter” or “bitterness,” the third son of Levi.
biblical_def: Merari was the third son of Levi (Gen 46:11), and the head of the Merarites, one of the three great Levitical families. To the Merarites was given the charge of the framework of the tabernacle: the boards, the bars, the pillars, the sockets, the pins, and the cords, with all the instruments thereof (Num 4:31–32). Theirs was the heaviest and most solid of the burdens, the bones and timbers that held up the whole structure of the sanctuary; they carried it upon four wagons drawn by eight oxen, under the hand of Ithamar (Num 7:8). While the Kohathites bore the holy vessels and the Gershonites the curtains, the Merarites bore the boards and pillars that gave the tabernacle its standing strength. The great singers Ethan and Jeduthun were of the house of Merari. When the Levites received their cities, the Merarites were given twelve cities among the tribes (Josh 21:7, 40). Merari’s name, “bitter,” perhaps recalls the bitterness of Egypt or of life in the world; yet his house bore the very framework of the dwelling of God. Merari stands at the head of the family that upheld the structure of the sanctuary, a witness that the unseen, load-bearing labours are as needful to the house of God as the visible and the beautiful.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of the unseen, load-bearing labours in the house of God. The Merarites bore the boards and pillars, the heavy framework that gave the tabernacle its standing strength — not the holy vessels nor the beautiful curtains, but the bones of the structure. The hidden, weighty work that upholds the church is as needful as the visible and the lovely; the LORD assigns such burdens by name and honours those who bear them.

Merari’s name, “bitter,” set over a house given to upholding the dwelling of God, also reminds the reader that the LORD takes what is bitter and consecrates it to His service. From the house of bitterness came the bearers of the sanctuary’s framework and the singers of His praise. So God turns the bitter things of His people’s lives to the upholding of His house and the music of His worship.

etymology: Hebrew Yitshar, “shining oil” or “anointing oil,” a son of Kohath and father of Korah.
biblical_def: Izhar was the second son of Kohath, and thus a grandson of Levi, the brother of Amram from whom came Aaron and Moses (Ex 6:18). His sons were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri (Ex 6:21). Izhar is chiefly remembered as the father of Korah, the Levite who led the great rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, gathering Dathan, Abiram, and two hundred and fifty princes of the congregation to challenge the priesthood, saying that all the congregation was holy and that Moses and Aaron took too much upon themselves (Num 16). For this presumption the earth opened and swallowed Korah and his company, and fire devoured the two hundred and fifty. Yet the line of Izhar through Korah was not wholly cut off, for the sons of Korah did not die (Num 26:11), and from them descended faithful singers and doorkeepers of the house of God, to whom several Psalms are ascribed. Izhar’s name, linked to anointing oil, sits in solemn contrast to his son’s rebellion against the anointed of the LORD. His house holds both the warning of Korah’s presumption and the mercy by which his line was preserved to sing the praises of God.
webster_summary: A son of Kohath and father of Korah, who led rebellion against Moses; yet the sons of Korah were spared.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his house holds both Korah’s warning and the mercy that spared his line.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning of Korah, the son of Izhar, who despised his Levitical honour and grasped at the priesthood, claiming that all the congregation was holy and that Moses and Aaron took too much upon themselves. This was rebellion against the order God Himself had appointed, and the earth swallowed him. To reject God’s appointed ministry under the pretence of a general holiness is presumption that ends in ruin.

Yet the mercy that spared the sons of Korah shines beside the judgment on their father. Though Korah perished, his children did not die, and from his line came faithful singers and doorkeepers, to whom several Psalms are ascribed. The LORD does not visit the rebellion of the father upon penitent children; out of the house of the rebel He raised up worshippers, that His praise might rise from the very line that once rose against Him.

etymology: Hebrew Uzzi’el, “God is my strength,” a son of Kohath and uncle of Aaron.
biblical_def: Uzziel was the fourth son of Kohath, a grandson of Levi, and the uncle of Aaron (Ex 6:18). His sons were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Zithri (Ex 6:22). Uzziel’s house comes into solemn view on the day that Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, were struck dead for offering strange fire before the LORD; for Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and bade them carry the bodies of their kinsmen from before the sanctuary out of the camp (Lev 10:4–5). Thus it fell to the house of Uzziel to perform the grievous office of bearing away the dead who had sinned in the very presence of God, while Aaron and his remaining sons were forbidden to mourn or to leave the sanctuary. The Uzzielites were numbered among the Kohathite Levites who served in the tabernacle, and in David’s day their descendants had their place among the courses of the Levites (1Ch 23:12, 20). Uzziel’s name, “God is my strength,” is a fitting confession for a house called to a hard and holy duty. He stands as a witness that the service of God sometimes lays upon His people grievous tasks, and that strength for such duties is found in the LORD alone.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the service of God sometimes lays grievous tasks upon His people. It fell to the sons of Uzziel to bear away the bodies of Nadab and Abihu, struck dead for their presumption, while the priests themselves were forbidden to mourn. Some holy duties are heavy and sorrowful; yet they too must be done, and the strength for them is found in the LORD, whom Uzziel’s very name confesses to be his strength.

The carrying away of Nadab and Abihu also stands as a warning bound up with Uzziel’s house, for it followed their offering of strange fire that God commanded not. The judgment fell within the family of Levi itself, that all might learn the LORD will be sanctified in them that come near Him. Nearness to the holy demands the deepest obedience; the same house that served the sanctuary bore away the kinsmen who profaned it.
roots_summary: The name means “God is my strength,” a fitting confession for a house called to hard duty.

etymology: Hebrew Amram, “exalted people” or “kindred of the exalted One,” the father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.
biblical_def: Amram was the eldest son of Kohath and grandson of Levi (Ex 6:18), the husband of Jochebed his father’s sister, and the father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (Ex 6:20; Num 26:59). Through Amram came the high priesthood, in Aaron, and the prophet and lawgiver who led Israel out of Egypt, in Moses; no man in the Old Testament was father to a more honoured family. Amram lived an hundred thirty and seven years (Ex 6:20). Little is told of him personally, yet the faith of his house is praised, for it was by faith that the parents of Moses hid him three months, not afraid of the king’s commandment, when they saw he was a goodly child (Heb 11:23). The piety of Amram and Jochebed, who feared God rather than Pharaoh, was honoured in the deliverer they brought forth and preserved. Amram stands as a witness to the great things that flow from a faithful and God-fearing household. From his quiet house came the priest who would stand between the people and God, the prophet who would speak with God face to face, and the prophetess who led the women in praise at the sea. The faith of the parents bore fruit in the generation that followed.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his house witnesses the great things that flow from a faithful, God-fearing family.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the fruit of a faithful and God-fearing household. From the quiet house of Amram and Jochebed came Aaron the high priest, Moses the lawgiver, and Miriam the prophetess. By faith they hid the infant Moses, fearing God rather than Pharaoh; and the LORD honoured their faith in the deliverer they brought forth. The piety of parents bears fruit in the generation that follows.

Amram’s house also shows that God prepares His great instruments in obscure and humble homes. There was nothing outwardly grand about a Levite household in bondage in Egypt; yet from it came the men who would shape the whole history of God’s people. The LORD often hides His mightiest works in the faithfulness of ordinary families, and brings forth deliverers from the homes of those who fear Him.

etymology: Hebrew Avihu, “he is my father” or “worshipper of God,” the second son of Aaron, slain for offering strange fire.
biblical_def: Abihu was the second son of Aaron the high priest, the brother of Nadab, Eleazar, and Ithamar (Ex 6:23). He was among those privileged to draw near to God on Mount Sinai, for Nadab and Abihu went up with Moses and Aaron and the seventy elders and saw the God of Israel, and did eat and drink in His presence (Ex 24:9–11). Yet this high honour did not keep him from presumption. On the day the priesthood was consecrated, Nadab and Abihu took every man his censer, and put fire therein, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which He commanded them not; and there went out fire from the LORD and devoured them, and they died before the LORD (Lev 10:1–2). Their sin was to bring into the worship of God a fire He had not appointed, presuming to serve Him after their own will rather than His command. Their bodies were carried out of the camp by the sons of Uzziel, and Aaron held his peace. Abihu stands as one of the gravest warnings in all Scripture against will-worship: that those who come near to God, however high their privilege, must serve Him only in the way He commands, for the LORD will be sanctified in them that draw nigh unto Him.
webster_summary: The second son of Aaron, slain with his brother Nadab for offering strange fire the LORD commanded not.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; his death is a grave warning against will-worship in the service of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the deadly seriousness of will-worship. Nadab and Abihu brought into the worship of God a fire He had not appointed, serving Him after their own invention rather than His command, and fire from the LORD devoured them. The lesson is plain and abiding: God must be worshipped only in the way He has commanded, not in ways men devise for themselves. What He has not commanded in His worship, He has forbidden.

Abihu’s high privilege, having seen the God of Israel at Sinai, made his presumption the more solemn, for nearness to God did not excuse him but increased his accountability. “I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me” (Lev 10:3) is the word that explains his death. This account is among the clearest foundations of the regulative principle of worship, that the LORD alone defines how He is to be approached, and that strange fire — worship of human invention — is an abomination to Him.
